manufacturer.olivetti.history:
Olivetti began in Ivrea, northern Italy, in 1908, when Camillo Olivetti founded a typewriter company. Under his son Adriano, the factory also became a social project: industrial buildings, housing and services for workers were part of a shared vision of community. This connection between technology, design and everyday life helps explain the character of the company's later computers.

The move into computing came in the 1950s. A team led by Mario Tchou developed the ELEA 9003, unveiled in 1959: a large transistor-based electronic computer intended for business data processing. Its design, by Ettore Sottsass, also considered how it would be installed and used. Even the power cables ran overhead rather than beneath a special floor, making the system easier to rearrange. Aesthetics went hand in hand with practical engineering decisions.

Acquisitions also supported expansion. The investment in Underwood, begun in 1959, brought a historic American typewriter brand and an extensive sales network into the group. Its main contribution to this story was commercial and industrial: it opened another route for selling Olivetti products in the United States. Restoring its facilities, however, proved more expensive than expected.

This venture soon faced a difficult period. Adriano died in 1960 and Tchou in 1961; the company also faced financial problems. In 1964, the electronics division was transferred to a company 75% controlled by General Electric. Olivetti sold its remaining stake in 1968 but continued developing small systems and terminals. Its computing story followed a different path from that of large computer centres.

The Programma 101, introduced in 1965, embodied that alternative: having a programmable machine on one's own desk. Developed by Pier Giorgio Perotto's team, with an exterior designed by Mario Bellini, it could store programs and data on magnetic cards. It is often called “the first personal computer”, although that label depends on the definition of a PC: the Computer History Museum places it on the boundary between a programmable calculator and a computer. Its importance lies in bringing programmed calculation to individual users before microprocessors became widespread.

In the 1970s, this desktop computing existed alongside several specialised product lines. The Audit A5 and A7 served accounting needs, while the TC800 machines were banking terminals. The P6060 and P6040 addressed technical and scientific computing. The P6060 combined BASIC programming, floppy disks and a built-in printer; the P6040 occupied a lower tier and incorporated an Intel 8080 microprocessor. These were different answers to specific tasks, before the general-purpose PC became widespread and could take on a new role simply by installing another program.

The M20 of 1982 opened another chapter, with a 16-bit Zilog processor and the PCOS operating system. It was an independent approach in a market beginning to gather around the IBM PC. Its incompatibility with that environment restricted access to an increasingly important range of software: choosing a computer also meant choosing which programs one could use.

With the M24, introduced in 1984, Olivetti changed course and embraced IBM compatibility and MS-DOS. The machine combined that compatibility with higher performance than the original PC, while the AT&T alliance opened an important sales channel in the United States. It became one of the brand's major computing successes: an office computer could draw on the compatible PC software market while retaining its own design.

The same platform could travel under several names. In 1981, Olivetti had acquired control of France's Logabax and Switzerland's Hermes Precisa, the latter associated with typewriters. Logabax subsequently offered the M24 in France as the Persona 1600: in this case, the product passed from the Italian parent to the acquired brand. In the United States it was sold as the AT&T PC 6300 through a commercial and equity alliance; AT&T was not a company bought by Olivetti.

The professional range continued to grow. The M28 took the range to the 80286, and the M380 to the 80386DX; the latter also had a compact version, the M380 C. The M300 designation covered other variants, including the 386-generation M300-30 and M300-30P. These names are best understood as part of a range with different formats and revisions, rather than assuming that each number marks a direct replacement for its predecessor. Olivetti adapted its desktops to successive PC generations while retaining different options in the catalogue.

The PCS models show another way of organising that range: compact machines with tiered performance. The PCS 86 combined a NEC V30, from the 8086-compatible generation, with integrated VGA graphics; the PCS 286 and PCS 386SX offered a move to newer processors in similarly compact machines. This helps explain their coexistence: a machine with an older architecture could still be equipped for office tasks, while other models offered greater capabilities. Belonging to the same commercial family did not mean sharing the same motherboard.

The acquisition of control of Acorn in 1985 brought another computing tradition into the group: that of a British company closely associated with education. Its BBC Master Compact had an Italian version, the Olivetti Prodest PC 128 S. The relationship also had a wider technological dimension: Acorn continued its own development and launched the ARM-based Archimedes computers in 1987. These were Acorn developments within the group, with their own identity; the acquisition does not turn their creators into an Ivrea design team.

Prodest brought several approaches to home and educational computing. The PC 128 came from the Thomson MO6, and the PC 128 S from Acorn: the added letter indicated a different platform, not a simple upgrade. The first machine's Thomson origins reflected a product relationship, not an Olivetti acquisition of Thomson. The PC 1 of 1987 took a third direction, IBM compatibility and MS-DOS, with the computer built into the keyboard case; the PC 1 HD with a hard disk followed later. The range thus brought together different approaches to the home market.

Mobility followed its own path. The M10 of 1983 was a small work tool with a tilting LCD screen; the M21 of 1984 aimed to make a more desktop-like system transportable, with a built-in monitor and a keyboard that closed over it. The M15 of 1987 combined PC compatibility with an LCD, although its roughly six kilograms are a reminder of how relative the term “portable” was at the time. These machines met different needs: carrying a lightweight tool or moving a more complete workstation.

The purchase of Triumph-Adler from Volkswagen in 1986 also left its mark on the ranges. The Dario 286 and Dario 386SX illustrate the connections between desktops from the two brands and Olivetti's PCS models. In addition, the German subsidiary was commissioned in 1990 to develop a new portable range, working with Y-E Data. The result was Olivetti 1., introduced in 1991 with 286 and 386 machines. The acquisition therefore brought development and manufacturing capabilities: this family was created after the purchase, rather than arriving with it as a range of finished products.

In the 1990s, the Quaderno of 1992 took that pursuit to an A5 format, weighing around one kilogram, and even included voice-recording functions. The Quaderno 33 followed in 1993 with higher performance. The Philos and Echos families, meanwhile, developed a more conventional notebook offering; the Echos even had a brick-red case option. Attention to form remained evident as portable computers began to look much more like those we know today.

In 1997, restructuring led the group to sell its personal computer business as telecommunications gained prominence. The shift culminated in the acquisition of control of Telecom Italia in 1999. The Olivetti brand remained associated with office products and services and reappeared on computers in later periods; 1997 therefore marks the end of an industrial chapter, not the disappearance of the name.

The company also left a legacy beyond its machines. Ivrea's industrial complex was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2018. It preserves the setting of a company that made the transition from mechanics to electronics while exploring its own relationship between factory, city and workers.
manufacturer.olivetti.description: Italian company founded in Ivrea and first known for its typewriters. Its computer business combined in-house engineering, industrial design and several families of IBM-compatible systems.
